notes.meaning: God gave Moses instructions to consecrate Aaron and his sons, which means to set them apart for holy service as priests. They were not allowed to appoint themselves, because priests had to be chosen and called by God. Moses was told to prepare one young bull and two rams with no defects, pointing to the pure offering God requires.

Along with the animals, Moses had to bring three kinds of bread made from fine wheat flour and oil, but without yeast. Bread without yeast represented purity, because yeast was often seen as a sign of decay or corruption. All these loaves and wafers were placed into a single basket and brought to God together with the sacrificial animals.

Aaron and his sons were brought to the entrance of the sacred tent, standing right between God's dwelling and the people they would serve. Moses washed their entire bodies with water before they could begin their work. This washing showed that anyone who comes near to serve a holy God must be completely cleansed from sin.

Moses dressed Aaron in the special, beautiful clothing made for the high priest. These holy garments showed that a priest must be clothed with righteousness and the gifts of God's Spirit rather than human pride. Placing the turban and the golden crown on his head showed that his sacred office was an honor given by God.

Moses poured sacred scented oil generously over Aaron's head so that it ran down. Pouring oil showed that God was pouring out His Holy Spirit to equip and enable Aaron for his heavy duties. It also taught the people that any true spiritual work must be blessed and guided by God.

Aaron's sons were also brought forward and dressed in plain linen tunics, sashes, and headbands to prepare them for active work. The Hebrew word for ordaining them meant filling their hands, showing that God was giving them sacred work to do for Him. God promised that the priesthood would stay in Aaron's family line for generations to come.

The young bull was brought before the sanctuary as a sin offering to make things right between God and the priests. Aaron and his sons pressed their hands onto the animal's head to identify themselves with it. By doing this, they confessed that they were guilty sinners who deserved death and asked God to let the animal take their place.

Moses killed the bull in the open courtyard in front of the Lord and before all the people. Because Aaron and his sons were not yet fully ordained, Moses carried out the priestly duty of slaughtering the sacrifice. This open offering showed that sin is a serious matter that must be dealt with publicly before God.

Moses dipped his finger into the bull's blood and smeared it onto the raised corners, or horns, of the bronze altar. The rest of the blood was poured out at the bottom of the altar. Smearing the blood on the horns cleansed and dedicated the altar itself so that it was ready for holy service.

The internal fat around the organs and the kidneys were taken and burned entirely on the altar. In the ancient world, fat was seen as the richest and best part of an animal. Offering it in fire meant giving the very best portion directly to the Lord.

The rest of the bull—its meat, skin, and waste—had to be carried outside the camp and burned completely to ashes. Usually priests could eat part of a sin offering, but not when the offering was for their own sins. This complete destruction showed that these earthly sacrifices could not truly remove the priests' own sin, pointing forward to a greater sacrifice to come.

Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the first ram, this time to offer a burnt offering. Instead of confessing guilt as with the sin offering, this action meant they were offering their whole lives to God. Moses slaughtered the ram and splashed its blood against all four sides of the altar to dedicate the gift to the Lord.

The ram was cut into pieces and washed thoroughly so that the entire animal was clean before being placed on the fire. Moses burned every part of it on the altar so that nothing was left behind. God called this a pleasing aroma, which is a picture meaning that He warmly and gladly accepted their complete surrender.

The second ram was the special ordination ram, celebrating the new fellowship between God and His priests. Moses took its blood and touched the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe of Aaron and each son. This showed that their whole bodies belonged to God—their ears to hear His word, their hands to do His work, and their feet to walk in His ways.

Moses gathered blood from the altar and mixed it with holy anointing oil, then sprinkled it over the priests and their clothes. The blood pictured forgiveness of sins, while the oil pictured the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit. Having both on their garments marked Aaron and his sons as completely dedicated to God's holy service.

Moses took the best fat parts of the second ram, its right thigh, and one of each kind of unleavened bread from the basket. Normally, the thigh belonged to the priest as food, but here it was set aside to be given back to God. These portions prepared the priests for the next step, where these gifts would be placed directly into their hands to present to the Lord.
